title: How Often Does Medicare Require a PT Progress Note?
summary: Medicare requires a PT progress note at least once every 10 treatment days. See what the report must include and how it differs from a re-evaluation.
body_markdown:
## How often does Medicare require a PT progress note?


At least once every 10 treatment days. A clinician has to write it, which in outpatient PT means the therapist who provides the services and supervises the assistant. The referring or supervising provider doesn’t have to sign it. Medicare sets the rule in the Benefit Policy Manual, Chapter 15, section 220.3.


**Treatment days, not calendar days.** A treatment day is one calendar day on which treatment, an eval, or a re-eval was provided, so two visits in a day still count as one. Your first reporting period starts on the first day of the episode, whether that day’s service was the eval or treatment. The period ends on the 10th treatment day or on a date you pick, whichever comes first, and the next treatment day opens the next one.


Days the patient doesn’t see anyone don’t count as treatment days, though an absence doesn’t excuse the report. A PTA can write elements between your reports. Those aren’t complete progress notes, and you still write one every period.


## What a Medicare progress report must contain


The manual spells out the elements. Here they are, grouped the way they actually fall.


**Every progress report carries:**


- The dates the reporting period began and ended
- The date you wrote it, which doesn’t have to fall inside the period
- Your signature and professional identification
- Objective reports of what the patient told you, where relevant
- Objective measurements against each goal you’re currently treating, or a description of what changed


**Because a clinician writes it, yours also carries:**


- Your assessment of improvement and how far the patient has progressed toward each goal, or hasn’t
- Your plan for continuing treatment, any additional evaluation results, and any revisions to the plan of care


That second pair is the part a PTA can’t supply. Assistants can report what they measured and what the patient said. They can’t make the clinical judgment about why progress happened or didn’t. The manual draws the line with its own example: “increasing strength” is not an objective measurement, and “patient ambulates 15 feet with maximum assistance” is.


The headings repeat every period. What goes under them can’t. PTs say the same thing about daily notes: copying forward is fine as long as something actually changed, because otherwise, why is the patient still coming in?


Identical notes get noticed. Clinicians describe them as a reliable way to draw scrutiny from insurers and from Medicare, and a progress report carries more weight than a daily note, because this is where you justify that skilled therapy is still necessary.


## Progress note vs. re-evaluation


These two get used interchangeably, and they aren’t the same kind of thing. One is a document. The other is a service you perform and then document.


Progress report Re-evaluation


What it is Documentation of care you already gave A service you perform, then document


How it’s paid Not billed separately Billed with its own code, 97164


When it’s due Every 10 treatment days Only when something has changed


Routine by design? Yes No


A progress report comes due on a schedule. A re-evaluation comes due when something happens. The manual is direct about it: continuous assessment of a patient’s progress is part of ongoing therapy and isn’t payable as a re-evaluation, and a re-evaluation is not a routine, recurring service.


What makes one payable is a reason: new clinical findings, a significant change in the patient’s condition, or failure to respond to the interventions in the plan of care. Your documentation has to show the change wasn’t anticipated in the plan of care you’re working from, and that’s the part that gets missed. A re-eval can also be appropriate before a planned discharge, to establish whether goals were met or to hand the patient off to whoever treats them next.


What doesn’t make one payable is the calendar.

## Where the rule comes from


Everything above comes from one place: the[Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, Chapter 15, section 220.3](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/downloads/bp102c15.pdf) , which covers documentation requirements for therapy services. It’s short enough to read in full, and worth doing once. CMS revises the chapter periodically, so check the revision date at the top when you go looking.


For practice detail rather than payment rules,[APTA’s documentation guidance](https://www.apta.org/your-practice/documentation) is the better resource. It covers documentation across the episode of care and points back to the manual for the Medicare-specific pieces.
